title: How Can We Improve Teachers?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles argues that instructional coaching misses half its potential impact because it focuses almost exclusively on teaching technique while ignoring curriculum — the tasks, models, explanations, success criteria, and retrieval sequences students encounter. His central claim is 'curriculum is queen': improving the curriculum lifts all teachers simultaneously, while individual teaching feedback is capped at a single teacher's practice. Salles proposes a scoring framework for prioritising coaching feedback: does this change make students work harder, improve the curriculum, or improve how hard students think? He argues coaches should choose 2-3 linked work-ons rather than a single silver bullet, and should frame improvement as a team project — where teachers at high-performance habits help those still acquiring them — rather than as an individual coach dragging each teacher uphill.
points: Coaching teachers normally focuses entirely on teaching, missing the 50% of what makes a difference that lives in the curriculum — the tasks, models, explanations, success criteria, retrieval, and practice students encounter.

Curriculum has a multiplier effect that teaching feedback doesn't: fix an aspect of the curriculum and you improve outcomes for all teachers and all students simultaneously, making curriculum fixes higher-leverage than individual teaching fixes.

Salles's three-point scoring framework for coaching feedback: 5 points if it makes students work hard, 4 points if it improves the curriculum, 3 points if it improves how hard students think — the highest-impact observations hit all three.
The right number of simultaneous work-ons is 2-3, each attached to already-existing routines (habit stacking) so they are cognitively manageable and can be practised multiple times daily.

The most effective improvement model is team-based: teachers already strong in target habits help those still developing them, turning a lonely top-down coaching model into collective professional development.
quotes: Coaching teachers normally focuses entirely on teaching — it misses 50% of what makes a difference: the curriculum. Curriculum means the tasks, models, explanations, success criteria, retrieval and practice students encounter in the lesson. To ignore this is crazy.

Teaching is king, but curriculum is queen, and she wears the trousers. It doesn't matter how brilliant your teaching is, if your retrieval curriculum doesn't make students remember it, they will learn less.
If you improve an aspect of the curriculum, you improve it for all teachers and all students. So curriculum fixes take precedent over all teaching fixes (except for real behaviour issues).
3 habits are not overwhelming. These habits are easy to acquire, because they are attached to already successful routines. This is habit stacking, a core concept from James Clear's Atomic Habits.

You are focusing on these as a team because this is what is going to lead to the most progress for all your students. Teachers who are brilliant at these are going to help those who aren't yet brilliant. You can rehearse these techniques in a department meeting.
The best way to ask yourself what feedback to give: 'What will have most impact on the progress of students if what I am seeing is typical of all the teacher's lessons?'
